steps.title: Install pandas and import it
steps.instructions: Install pandas, create main.py with import pandas as pd, build a DataFrame and Series and run it; then in a notebook load the downloaded CSV with pd.read_csv and inspect, select (.loc/.iloc), filter, modify, drop, clean (isnull/dropna/fillna) and group (groupby) it. Run each cell to see the output.

targets.caption: Install pandas from the terminal
Import pandas with the pd alias
Build a DataFrame from a dict of lists
Printed Series shows index, values and dtype
Load the CSV into a DataFrame
Label-based selection with .loc
Position-based selection with .iloc
Boolean mask selecting matching rows
Remove columns or rows with drop()
Count missing values per column
Drop or fill missing values
Group by a column and aggregate

explanations.topic: Using pandas from a Python file vs a Jupyter notebook
Installing pandas with pip (pip3 on Mac/Linux)
Using a uv virtual environment and uv run
Why pandas is imported as pd
pandas has two main types: DataFrame and Series
A DataFrame is a 2D table with labeled rows and columns

hints: Open a terminal in an empty project folder and install pandas first.
Run `pip install pandas` (or `pip3 install pandas` on Mac/Linux); with uv, run `uv init .` then `uv add pandas`.
Create main.py and write `import pandas as pd` as its first line.
Run it with `python main.py` or `uv run main.py`; no output and no traceback means the import works.
Import pandas with `import pandas as pd`. Then build a DataFrame and a Series.
Make a dict whose keys are column names and whose values are equal-length lists, then pass it to pd.DataFrame(...).
Create pd.Series([...]) from a plain list, print both objects, and run `python main.py`.
If you get a ValueError, check that every list in the dict has the same length.
Make sure your notebook is using the Python environment where pandas and ipykernel are installed (pick the kernel in the top-right).
Download the CSV from the techwithtim/PanadasTutorial GitHub repo and put it in the same folder as your .ipynb file.
Use a relative path in pd.read_csv("yourfile.csv"), and put df alone on the last line of the cell to display it.
If the table is truncated, that's normal: Jupyter shows the first and last rows plus a 'N rows × M columns' footer.
Make sure the cell that loads the CSV into df has been run first in this notebook session.
head() and tail() show the first and last 5 rows by default; pass a number like df.head(10) to see more.
info() and describe() are methods and need parentheses; shape is an attribute and has none.
Run each command in its own cell so every output is displayed. Only the last expression in a cell is shown automatically.
A single column comes back as a Series with df["name"]. For several columns, pass a list inside the brackets: df[["a", "b"]].
Use df.loc[...] when you select rows by index label, and df.iloc[...] when you select by integer position.
Both accept a row part and a column part: df.loc[0:3, ["a", "b"]] or df.iloc[0:3, 0:2]. A loc slice includes its end label. An iloc slice excludes its end position.
If you get a KeyError, print df.columns and copy the exact column name, including case and spaces.
Put a comparison like df["col"] > value inside df[...]. The comparison gives a True/False Series, and df[...] keeps only the True rows.
To combine conditions, wrap each one in its own parentheses and join them with & (and) or | (or).
Python's 'and' and 'or' keywords don't work on Series. Use & and | instead.
Run the cell. The output should show only the rows that match, keeping their original index labels.
Change a single cell by assigning through .loc with a row label and a column name.
Make a computed column by assigning an expression built from existing columns to df["new_name"].
drop() returns a new DataFrame. Pass columns=[...] for columns or index=[...] for rows, then reassign the result or display it.
Finish the cell with df on its own line so the updated table is shown.
Start by finding out where data is missing. Call isnull() on the DataFrame and chain .sum() to count the gaps in each column.
Run df.isnull().sum(). The output lists each column with a count and ends with 'dtype: int64'.
Next, either remove incomplete rows with df = df.dropna() or replace the gaps with df = df.fillna(value).
dropna and fillna return a new DataFrame. Assign the result back to df, or pass inplace=True. Then display df to confirm the change.
Pick a column with repeated values, like a category, and group by it.
Call an aggregation after groupby, for example df.groupby("col").mean(), and run the cell.
If mean() fails on text columns, select a numeric column first, or use .mean(numeric_only=True).
Try df.sort_values("col") or df["col"].value_counts() to rank and count values.
common_mistakes: Installing pandas into one Python interpreter and running the file with another, which gives ModuleNotFoundError.
Using `pip` on Mac/Linux where only `pip3` points at Python 3.
Running `python main.py` instead of `uv run main.py` after installing pandas only into the uv virtual environment.
Naming the file pandas.py, which shadows the real pandas module.
Typing `uv add pandas` before running `uv init .` in the folder.
Lists in the dict have different lengths, which raises a ValueError ("All arrays must be of the same length").
Writing pd.dataframe or pd.series in lowercase. The classes are DataFrame and Series.
Creating the objects but forgetting to print() them in a .py script, so nothing appears.
pandas not installed in the interpreter being used, which raises ModuleNotFoundError.
Saving the GitHub page HTML instead of the raw CSV (use the Raw/download button), which causes parsing errors.
CSV placed in a different folder than the notebook, giving FileNotFoundError.
Selecting a kernel without pandas installed, giving ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'.
Writing print(df) or forgetting to put df on the last line, so the rich table is not shown.
Typo in the filename or extension (e.g. .csv.txt).
Writing df.shape() with parentheses, which raises TypeError: 'tuple' object is not callable.
Putting several commands in one cell and seeing only the last result.
Restarting the kernel without rerunning the read_csv cell, which causes NameError: name 'df' is not defined.
Expecting describe() to include text columns; by default it summarizes only numeric columns.
Using single brackets with several names, e.g. df["a", "b"], which raises a KeyError instead of returning two columns.
Calling .loc/.iloc with parentheses instead of square brackets.
Passing column names to .iloc or integer positions to .loc for columns.
Expecting df.loc[0:3] to return 3 rows. A loc slice includes the end label, so it returns 4.
Misspelling a column name or getting its case wrong, which leads to a KeyError.
Using 'and'/'or' instead of &/|, which raises 'ValueError: The truth value of a Series is ambiguous'.
Leaving out the parentheses around each condition. Operator precedence then makes & bind before >, which causes a TypeError or wrong results.
Misspelling a column name inside the mask, which raises a KeyError.
Comparing a numeric column against a string value, for example "10" instead of 10.
Using chained indexing like df["col"][0] = v, which triggers SettingWithCopyWarning and may not update df.
Calling df.drop("col") without axis=1 or columns=, which raises KeyError because it looks for a row label.
Forgetting that drop() is not in-place, so the column still appears afterwards.
Misspelling a column name in .loc, which silently creates a new column instead of updating the existing one.
Calling df.dropna() without assigning the result, so df still contains the missing values.
Writing df.isnull without parentheses, which shows the method object instead of the counts.
Using dropna when most rows have a missing value somewhere, which leaves an almost empty DataFrame.
Calling fillna with no argument, which raises a ValueError because it needs a value or method.
Calling groupby without an aggregation. That only shows a DataFrameGroupBy object, not a table.
Using mean() on non-numeric columns in newer pandas, which raises a TypeError.
Misspelling the column name, which raises a KeyError.
Expecting sort_values to change df in place without reassigning it or passing inplace=True.
steps.code:
import pandas as pd
import pandas as pd

data = {
    "Name": ["Tim", "Joe", "Sarah"],
    "Age": [25, 30, 28],
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df)

series = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(series)
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
df
df.head()
df.tail()
df.info()
df.describe()
df.shape
df["column_name"]
df[["column_1", "column_2"]]
df.loc[0]
df.loc[0:3, ["column_1", "column_2"]]
df.iloc[0]
df.iloc[0:3, 0:2]
df[df["col"] > value]
df[(df["col"] > value) & (df["other"] == "x")]
df[(df["col"] > value) | (df["other"] == "x")]
df.loc[0, "col"] = value
df["new"] = ...
df = df.drop(columns=["new"])
df
df.isnull().sum()
df = df.dropna()
# or: df = df.fillna(0)
df
df.groupby("col").mean()
df.sort_values("col", ascending=False)
df["col"].value_counts()

steps.title: Load orders.csv into a DataFrame
steps.instructions: In an empty folder, download orders.csv from https://github.com/techwithtim/PanadasTutorial, run `uv init` and `uv add pandas`, then in main.py write `import pandas as pd`, `df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")` and `print(df)`. Run `uv run main.py` and confirm it prints 40 rows x 9 columns.

targets.caption: Load the CSV into a DataFrame
The printed DataFrame size

explanations.topic: What CSV files are and why pandas suits two-dimensional data
Headers become columns, values become rows
DataFrames as input to machine learning libraries
pd.read_csv loads a file into a DataFrame
Reading the printed table and its rows x columns summary

hints: Make sure orders.csv sits in the same folder as main.py, and that you ran uv add pandas.
Import pandas as pd, then call pd.read_csv with the file name as a string and store the result in df.
Print df, then run the script with uv run main.py.
The last line of the output should read [40 rows x 9 columns].

Typing pd.read_CSV or pd.readcsv instead of pd.read_csv
Running python main.py outside the uv environment so pandas isn't found

Creating a notebook via Command Palette or .ipynb file

hints: Create a file named notebook.ipynb (or use Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P → 'Create: New Jupyter Notebook') and save it next to orders.csv.
In the first cell write `import pandas as pd` and `df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")`, then run it and pick a Python kernel.
Add a new cell below with `print(df)` and run it; the table should end with '[N rows x M columns]'.

Do the same with df.tail() in another cell to see the bottom five rows.
common_mistakes: Saving the notebook with a .py extension instead of .ipynb, so no cells appear.
Not having the VS Code Python/Jupyter extension installed, so the notebook can't run.
Selecting a kernel/interpreter that doesn't have pandas or ipykernel installed (ModuleNotFoundError).
Running only the print cell first, giving NameError: name 'df' is not defined.
Saving notebook.ipynb in a different folder from orders.csv, causing FileNotFoundError.
Forgetting the parentheses (df.head instead of df.head()), which prints a method reference instead of a table

Putting head() and tail() in the same cell without print(), so only the last result is displayed

steps.title: Inspect types and summary statistics
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb run `df.info()` and `df.describe()` to see dtypes and summary statistics. Then run `df.columns` and `df.index` to list column names and the RangeIndex.

targets.caption: info() reports entries, columns and dtypes
describe() summary statistics table
List all column names
The index runs from start to stop by step

explanations.topic: df.info() shows entry count, column count and each column's dtype
Why text columns show as object rather than string
df.describe() generates descriptive statistics: central tendency, dispersion, shape
Reading the percentile rows (25%, 50%, 75%)
df.columns returns the column names as an Index
df.index is a RangeIndex with start, stop and step
Why these are the first commands run after loading a DataFrame

hints: Both are methods called on your DataFrame variable, each in its own cell.
Run df.info() to see the number of entries, columns and their dtypes.
Then run df.describe() to get count, mean, std, min, percentiles and max for numeric columns.
Remember the parentheses: df.info() and df.describe(), not df.info or df.describe.
Both are attributes, not methods: no parentheses needed.
In a new cell type df.columns and run it, then do the same with df.index.
Put each one in its own cell, or as the last line of a cell, so the notebook displays the result.
df.index should print something like RangeIndex(start=0, stop=N, step=1), where N is your row count.
common_mistakes: Leaving off the parentheses (df.describe), which prints the bound method instead of the table.
Expecting describe() to summarize text columns by default; it only covers numeric columns unless include='all' is passed.
Wrapping info() in print(), which prints its output followed by an extra 'None'.
Running the cells before the cell that loads the CSV into df, which causes a NameError.
Writing df.columns() or df.index(), which raises TypeError because these are attributes.
Putting both on non-final lines of one cell, so only the last one is displayed.
Misspelling the attribute, for example df.column, which raises AttributeError.
Running the cells before running the cell that loads the CSV, which raises NameError for df.

steps.title: Load CSV and select a column
steps.instructions: In your empty folder run `pip install pandas jupyter`, download the orders CSV from https://github.com/techwithtim/PanadasTutorial into it, and in a new notebook (e.g. main.ipynb) run `import pandas as pd` and `df = pd.read_csv("<file>.csv")`. Print `df.columns`, select `df["Country"]` (a Series), try `len(...)` and `set(...)` on it, then select `df[["Country", "Product"]]` (a DataFrame).

targets.caption: Load the CSV into a DataFrame
List all column names first
Unique values via Python set
Pass a list of column names inside the brackets

explanations.topic: Selecting a column returns a pandas Series, not a DataFrame
DataFrames can be indexed by column as well as by row
Long Series output is truncated in the notebook
Plain Python len() and set() work on a Series
A list of column names selects multiple columns
A list returns a DataFrame, not a Series
One column name gives a Series, two or more give a DataFrame

hints: Run df.columns first so you can see the exact column names.
Select a column with square brackets and its name as a string: df["Country"].
Column names are case-sensitive and must match exactly, including spaces.
Wrap the selection in len(...) or set(...) to count rows or see unique values.
Inside the outer brackets, put a list of column names instead of a single name.
A list in Python uses its own square brackets, so you end up with two pairs of brackets.
Try df[["Country", "Product"]], using columns that exist in your CSV.
common_mistakes: Using a path to the CSV that doesn't match where the file was saved, causing FileNotFoundError.
Typing df[Country] without quotes, causing a NameError.
Misspelling or wrong capitalisation of the column name (e.g. "country"), causing a KeyError.
Calling df.columns() with parentheses — columns is an attribute, not a method.
Forgetting to run the import/read_csv cell before later cells, so df is undefined.
Writing df["Country", "Product"] with single brackets, which raises a KeyError because pandas looks for one tuple-named column
Misspelling a column name or getting its case wrong, which raises a KeyError
Expecting a Series back: a list of columns always returns a DataFrame
Assuming the original df was changed: the selection is a new DataFrame, so assign it to a variable if you need it later

df.columns

steps.title: Index rows with iloc
steps.instructions: In main.ipynb use `df.iloc[0]` and `df.iloc[10]` to get rows by position, and `list(df.iloc[10])` to convert one to a list. Access values by position or by column name, e.g. `df.iloc[10]["Country"]`.

targets.caption: Select the row at position 10 with iloc
Convert the row to a plain Python list
Access a value in the row by column name

explanations.topic: iloc selects rows by integer position
Converting a row to a list; pandas vs built-in types
Accessing row values by position or column name

hints: Columns use df[...], but rows by position use df.iloc[...].
Try df.iloc[0] to see the first row as a Series.
Wrap a row in list(...) to get its values as a Python list.
On a single row, index by a column name like row["Country"].
common_mistakes: Using parentheses df.iloc(0) instead of square brackets df.iloc[0].
Using df[0] or df.loc[...] when you mean position-based row access.
Requesting a position beyond the number of rows (IndexError).
Misspelling the column name when accessing a row value (KeyError is case-sensitive).

df.iloc[10]

steps.title: Filter rows with boolean conditions
steps.instructions: Filter rows with a boolean mask like `df[df["Category"] == "Electronics"]`, combine conditions with `&` and `|` in parentheses, then try numeric filters like `df[df["Quantity"] > 2]`, `<=` and `!=`; run each cell.

targets.caption: Filter rows where Category equals Electronics
Combine two conditions; each wrapped in parentheses
Numeric filter on Quantity

explanations.topic: A boolean condition inside df[...] keeps only matching rows
Empty result because the wrong column (Product vs Category) was used
Use a single & (not 'and') and wrap each condition in parentheses
Single pipe | means OR, returning rows matching either condition
Comparison operators >, <, <=, != work as numeric filters

hints: Look at your columns first (df.head()) and pick one to filter on, e.g. a category column.
A filter has the form df[df["Column"] == value]; the inner part builds a True/False mask.
To combine conditions, wrap each in parentheses and join with & (and) or | (or).
For numbers, try df[df["Quantity"] > 2], then swap the operator for <=, != and compare the results.
common_mistakes: Filtering the wrong column (e.g. Product instead of Category) and getting an empty table
Using Python's 'and'/'or' instead of & and |, which raises a ValueError about ambiguous truth value
Forgetting parentheses around each condition when using & or |, causing operator precedence errors
Misspelling a column name or value (case-sensitive, e.g. 'electronics' vs 'Electronics'), causing KeyError or no rows
Comparing a numeric column to a string like '2' instead of the number 2
steps.code:
df[df["Category"] == "Electronics"]
df[(df["Category"] == "Electronics") & (df["Country"] == "USA")]
df[(df["Category"] == "Electronics") | (df["Country"] == "USA")]
df[df["Quantity"] > 20]
df[df["Quantity"] > 2]
df[df["Quantity"] <= 2]
df[df["Quantity"] != 2]

steps.title: Filter with string methods and isin
steps.instructions: Filter with `.str.startswith("A")` and `.str.endswith("a")` on a text column, then `df[df["Country"].isin([...])]`, and negate it with `~` to get all other values.

targets.caption: String method filter on a text column
Filter by a list of values
Tilde reverses the isin condition

explanations.topic: str.startswith filters rows by string prefix
String matching is case-sensitive (endswith 'A' vs 'a')
Using .str to access string methods on a column
isin replaces a long combined OR condition
~ operator negates a boolean condition

hints: Access string methods on a column through .str, e.g. df["Customer Name"].str.startswith("A"), and wrap it in df[...] to filter.
Matching is case-sensitive: names end in a lowercase "a", so use .str.endswith("a").
isin takes a list: df[df["Country"].isin(["USA", "Sweden", "Brazil"])].
Put ~ before the condition inside the brackets to get the opposite rows: df[~df["Country"].isin([...])].
common_mistakes: Calling df["Customer Name"].startswith("A") without .str, which raises AttributeError.
Using endswith("A") with an uppercase A, which returns an empty DataFrame.
Passing several strings to isin instead of one list.
Using ! or not instead of ~ to negate the condition.
Misspelling the column name (e.g. "Customer name"), which causes a KeyError.
steps.code:
df[df["Customer Name"].str.startswith("A")]
df[df["Customer Name"].str.endswith("a")]
df[df["Country"].isin(["USA", "Sweden", "Brazil"])]
df[~df["Country"].isin(["USA", "Sweden", "Brazil"])]

steps.title: Update rows with loc
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, update a column for rows matching a condition with `df.loc[df["Customer Name"] == ..., "Product"] = ...` and display those rows to verify. Then rename countries with `df.loc[df["Country"] == "USA", "Country"] = "United States"` and check that no USA rows remain.

targets.caption: loc selects rows by condition and a column, then assigns a new value
Every USA row is renamed to United States in one statement

explanations.topic: loc locates rows by label or condition instead of by position like iloc
A loc filter returns a DataFrame because several rows can match
Adding a column after the comma and assigning updates those cells in place
One loc assignment updates every matching row (USA to United States)

hints: Start with df.loc[condition] to see which rows match before you change anything.
After the condition, add a comma and then the column name: df.loc[condition, "Product"].
Assign with =, for example df.loc[df["Country"] == "USA", "Country"] = "United States", then filter again to confirm.
common_mistakes: Using iloc with a boolean condition or a column name instead of loc
Chained assignment like df[cond]["Product"] = "Tim", which triggers SettingWithCopyWarning and doesn't change df
Misspelling the column ("Product Name" vs "Product"), which creates a new column instead of updating
Using = instead of == inside the condition
Re-running the USA filter after the rename and thinking the update failed because the result is empty
steps.code:
df.loc[df["Customer Name"] == "Anna ..."]
df.loc[df["Customer Name"] == "Anna ...", "Product"] = "Tim"
df.loc[df["Customer Name"] == "Anna ..."]
df.loc[df["Country"] == "USA", "Country"] = "United States"
df[df["Country"] == "USA"]
df[df["Country"] == "United States"]

steps.title: Uppercase a column with str.upper
steps.instructions: Overwrite a column with its uppercased values using `df["Col"] = df["Col"].str.upper()`. Display the column to confirm that every value is uppercase.

targets.caption: Overwrite the column with its uppercased values
Printed column shows all-uppercase values

explanations.topic: Assigning a transformed column back over the original column
Vectorized string methods via .str apply to every value in the column
Confirming that every value in the column was updated

hints: Use the column's .str accessor to get string methods that apply to every value.
Assign the result back to the same column: df["Country"] = ...
The full line is df["Country"] = df["Country"].str.upper(). Then run df["Country"] in a new cell to see the result.
common_mistakes: Calling df["Country"].upper() without .str, which raises AttributeError: 'Series' object has no attribute 'upper'.
Writing .str.upper without parentheses, which assigns a method object instead of the uppercased values.
Not assigning the result back, so df stays unchanged.
Using a column name with the wrong case (e.g. "country"), which raises a KeyError.
Running the display cell before the assignment cell.

steps.title: Clean data and rename columns
steps.instructions: In an empty folder, clone https://github.com/techwithtim/PanadasTutorial, `pip install pandas jupyter`, and in a notebook load the repo's CSV with `pd.read_csv`, then try `df.drop(39)`, `dropna()`, `fillna(0, inplace=True)`, `rename(columns={...})`, `value_counts()`, `groupby('Country')['Price'].sum()` and `sort_values('Price', ascending=False)`. Finally run `df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False)` and confirm new_file.csv appears in your folder.

targets.caption: Drop the row at index 39 and reassign to df
Fill missing values with 0 in place
Rename the order ID column
Count how many rows each country has
Total Price per Country
Sort rows from most to least expensive
Write the DataFrame to a new CSV file
The new file appears in the file explorer

explanations.topic: df.drop(label) removes the row with that index label and returns a new DataFrame, so the result is reassigned to df
Using df.tail() to confirm the row was removed
dropna removes rows containing null/NA values
fillna replaces missing values instead of removing rows
inplace=True modifies the existing DataFrame instead of returning a new one
Renaming columns with rename(columns=...)

groupby works like SQL GROUP BY
Summing price per country group
Sorting rows with sort_values and the ascending flag
ascending=False gives descending order, highest price first
Saving a modified DataFrame with df.to_csv
index=True vs index=False: whether the row index is written as a column

hints: drop returns a new DataFrame, so assign the result back: df = df.drop(...).
Pass the index label of the row to remove, here 39.
Finish the cell with df.tail() so the notebook displays the last rows.
If you get a KeyError, the label is not in the index. Reload the CSV and try again.
Start by reloading your CSV into df with pd.read_csv so you work from clean data.
df.dropna() drops rows with missing values; df.fillna(0, inplace=True) fills them with 0 instead.
Use df.rename(columns={'OldName': 'New Name'}, inplace=True) with the exact existing column name as the key.
Display df afterwards and check that the header row shows the new column name.
Select the country column first with square brackets, then call a method on it.
The method that tallies unique values is value_counts.
Type df['Country'].value_counts() in a new cell and run it (use your own column name if it differs).
Start from your DataFrame and call .groupby() with the column name you want to group on, as a string.
Select the column to aggregate with square brackets after groupby, e.g. ['Price'].
Finish with .sum() and run the cell: df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum()
DataFrames have a method that reorders rows by a column's values.
Use df.sort_values(...) and pass the name of your price column.
To put the largest values first, add ascending=False.

common_mistakes: Calling df.drop(39) without reassigning the result, so df is unchanged.
Running the drop cell twice, which raises KeyError: '[39] not found in axis'.
Passing a wrong path to read_csv. The path must point to the CSV inside the cloned repo folder.
Confusing the index label with the position after rows have already been removed.
Forgetting inplace=True (or not reassigning), so fillna/rename return a new DataFrame and df stays unchanged.
Misspelling the old column name in the rename dict: rename silently does nothing instead of raising an error.
Passing the dict directly, as in df.rename({'a':'b'}), without columns=, which renames index labels instead of columns.
Expecting df.dropna() alone to change df: without inplace=True or reassignment, the result is discarded.
Forgetting the parentheses: df['Country'].value_counts shows a bound method instead of counts.
Misspelling the column name or wrong case ('country' vs 'Country'), which raises KeyError.
Calling df.value_counts() on the whole DataFrame instead of the single column.
Using the old column name after renaming columns in the previous step.
Using a column name that does not match the renamed header exactly (case or spaces), causing a KeyError.
Writing .sum without parentheses, which prints a method object instead of totals.
Price column still stored as text (e.g. with '$'), so sum concatenates strings instead of adding numbers.
Calling df.groupby('Country').sum() without selecting Price, summing every column.
Leaving the default ascending=True, so the cheapest rows appear first.
Using the old column name after the columns were renamed in step 2, which raises a KeyError.
Writing ascending='False' as a string instead of the boolean False.
Expecting df itself to change: sort_values returns a new DataFrame unless you reassign it or use inplace=True.
Typing df.2csv or df.tocsv instead of df.to_csv (the presenter says "df.2 csv" aloud).
Forgetting quotes around the file name.
Leaving out index=False, which writes the index as an unnamed extra column.
Using the original file name and overwriting the source data.
Looking for the file in a different folder than the notebook's working directory.
